C1.title: The Scholarship That Needed an OTP
C1.brief: Anjali, 17, lost Rs. 8,000 from her family's savings. She says she followed instructions from what looked like an official scholarship programme. Her phone is the only evidence. Reconstruct what happened.
C1.closing: Anjali followed a well-built script. The attack succeeded because it was designed to defeat checking, not because she was careless.

C1-01.explain: No exam, no interview, Rs. 50,000 for anyone. Real scholarships ask you to apply and show you qualify.
C1-02.explain: Anyone can call themselves an officer. Look closely: a zero hides inside official, and the profile lists no organisation.
C1-03.explain: Real offices give you time. A 2-hour deadline is there to stop you from thinking or asking.
C1-04.explain: A code like this is a key. No real office ever needs you to read it out.
C1-05.explain: Rs. 8,000 left minutes after the call, to a person’s name. The code is what let it happen.
C1-06.explain: Once they have what they want, they delete or block. A vanishing page is a scam’s last step.
C1-G1.explain: A page only 2 weeks old with identical comments is a stage set. Real scholarships have a history.
C1-G2.explain: Secrecy keeps you from asking someone who might say: this looks wrong.
C1-G3.explain: Read the address slowly. It copies a real name and adds extra words. Do not tap it.
C1-X1.explain: The same number shows up on the page, in the chat and on the call. One person, three disguises.
C1-L1.q: Establish the origin. Anjali says this began with something she saw online. Which app holds the original offer, and what made it attractive?
C1-L1.nudge: Check what she saved for later.
C1-L2.q: Someone then contacted her as an officer. What evidence, if any, supports that identity?
C1-L2.nudge: Compare the account handle and profile details with what a real organisation would show.
C1-L3.q: Time pressure often decides these cases. Find the message that set a deadline.
C1-L3.nudge: Short alphanumeric sender names are SMS. Check the inbox.
C1-L4.q: A call came before the loss. Review the recording: what did the caller ask for?
C1-L4.nudge: Call recordings are attached to the call log.
C1-L5.q: Establish the loss. When did the money move, and to whom?
C1-L5.nudge: Check the transaction history in the payment app.
C1-L6.q: After the loss, compare the offer and the chat with how they looked earlier. What changed?
C1.fix.q: The caller asks Anjali to read out the code that just arrived by SMS. What is the correct response?
C1.fix.a: Read it out, because it is a scholarship.
C1.fix.a.why: Scholarships never need your code. Authority attached to the request changes nothing.
C1.fix.b: Hang up and never share the OTP.
C1.fix.b.why: Correct. An OTP authorises one specific action. Reading it out hands the attacker that approval.
C1.fix.c: Ask the caller to prove who he is.
C1.fix.c.why: Asking for proof does not help: proof can be fabricated, and the code remains a live approval.
C1.replay.1: Bait: an offer too generous to be real, with no application or exam.
C1.replay.2: Pretext: a named officer and a profile that lists no organisation.
C1.replay.3: Pressure: a two-hour deadline and an instruction to tell nobody.
C1.replay.4: Extraction: the one-time code is read out and Rs. 8,000 leaves.
C1.replay.5: Exit: the page, the post and the chat disappear.
C1.debrief.mechanism: The attacker built credibility in layers: a convincing page, a named officer on a second channel, then a scheduled call. When the caller asked for the code, a transfer was already waiting for approval. The OTP sent by the bank is that approval. The deadline and the instruction to tell no one meant there were two minutes and nobody to ask.
C1.debrief.c1: An OTP is an approval, not an identity check. Never read it to anyone, whoever they claim to be.
C1.debrief.c2: Verify an offer on the organisation's own website, found independently. Real scholarships require an application.
C1.debrief.c3: Treat any deadline combined with secrecy as a stop signal.
C1-P04-R4.explain: Her hesitation was right: the message itself said never to share the code. The caller's next line is designed to talk her out of that instinct.
C1-P04-R6.explain: This is the moment the attack succeeded. Nothing in her words is a red flag; the damage is that a live approval code has been read out.
C1-CH05b.explain: Setup, not yet an attack: asking her to keep the phone nearby prepares for the code request that comes later.
C1-CH05d.explain: Setup again: a scheduled call and an instruction not to be late keep her ready and under time pressure.
